STATEMENT
Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction.
They enjoy only the jurisdiction afforded to them by the
Constitution and Congress.  While Congress has given
federal district courts original  jurisdiction over cases involving federal questions, 28 U.S.C. § 1331, Congress has
not empowered district courts to exercise appellate jurisdiction to review and reject state-court judgments.  That
power rests solely with this Court.  Id. § 1257.

2

This Court’s decisions in Rooker, Feldman, and
Exxon distill this statutory framework into the rule that
“state-court losers” cannot seek “review and rejection” of
state-court judgments in federal district courts because to
do so would be “to exercise appellate jurisdiction over
state-court judgments.”  Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi
Basic Indus. Corp., 544 U.S. 280, 284, 292 (2005) (citation
omitted); see Rooker v. Fid. Tr. Co. , 263 U.S. 413 (1923);
D.C. Ct. of Appeals v. Feldman, 460 U.S. 462 (1983).
That rule resolves this case.  As the Fourth Circuit
recognized below, petitioner’s suit presents “the paradigm
situation in which Rooker-Feldman precludes a federal
district court from proceedin g.”  Pet.App.8a (quoting
Exxon, 544 U.S. at 293).  Petitioner and her five attorneys
sued in Maryland state court, resulting in a consent order
securing her discharge from respondent University of
Maryland Baltimore Washington Medical Center
(BWMC).  Petitioner, unsatisfied with that order, filed this
federal suit asking the district court to “void” the consent
order, then filed a state-court appeal of the consent order,
and then stayed her state-co urt appeal.  The court below
correctly concluded that peti tioner’s federal suit impermissibly seeks review and rejection of a state-court
judgment.
Petitioner does not dispu te that her suit would be
foreclosed had she exhausted review within the statecourt system before filing this  suit.  Petitioner (at 15) instead asserts that her federal suit is viable because the
challenged state-court judgment “remains subject to further review in state court.”  But the availability of further
state-court review makes federal-court intervention
worse, not better.  No precedent or statute supports petitioner’s theory that litigant s can procure federal district-

3

court appellate jurisdiction by jumping to federal court
before completing state-court appellate review.
Petitioner’s rule would flout federalism and comity
principles as old as the Nation by authorizing federal district-court interference with ongoing state-court
proceedings, even before state appellate courts have had
the opportunity to take a look.  If this Court must wait for
the state appellate process to play out before reviewing
state-court judgments, surely district courts cannot cut in
line to review them first.
A. Factual Background
1.  This case—along with seven others—arises out of
petitioner T.M.’s involuntary admission for inpatient psychiatric treatment at BWMC, a hospital operated by
respondent University of Maryland Medical System Corporation (UMMS).  UMMS has served Marylanders
through its predecessors since 1823.  A Historical Timeline, UMMS (2026), https://tinyurl.com/2u24w3vz.  Today,
UMMS cares for over one million patients each year
across myriad medical specialties.  System Overview ,
UMMS (2026), https://tinyurl.com/2wtruv3s.
Petitioner is one such pati ent.  She experiences episodes of psychosis, which her private physician attributes
to gluten sensitivity.  Pet. App.22a; J.A.11.  According to
petitioner, ingesting “any amount of gluten” changes her
mental status.  Pet.App.22a; J.A.28.  Other doctors, including respondent Dr. Thomas J. Cummings, have diagnosed
her with schizophrenia.  E.g., J.A.175.
In July 2022, petitioner “s igned an advance directive
form that was downloaded from the Maryland Attorney
General’s Office website.”  Doe v. Univ. of Md. Med. Sys.
Corp., 2025 WL 3553026, at *1 (4th Cir. Dec. 11, 2025).  Although the document attempted to designate petitioner’s

4

parents as her health care agents, it “failed to comply with
the statutory requirements fo r its creation,” because one
of the health care agents (petitioner’s mother) also witnessed the document.  Id. at *6; see Md. Code Ann.,
Health-Gen. § 5-602(c)(2)(ii).
2.  On March 23, 2023, police escorted petitioner to
BWMC for immediate evaluati on after she became psychotic, aggressive, and agitated.  Pet.App.22a; J.A.14.  The
hospital determined that peti tioner’s purported advance
directive was “not valid” under Maryland law and conducted an independent evaluation.  Compl. ¶ 32, Doe v.
Univ. of Md. Med. Sys. Corp., No. 23-cv-3318 (D. Md. Dec.
6. 2023), Dkt. 1 (“23-3318 Co mpl.”); Md. Code Ann.,
Health-Gen. § 10-624(b)(3).  Hospital staff diagnosed petitioner with schizophrenia an d concluded that involuntary
admission would best ensure her safety.  See 23-3318
Compl. ¶¶ 32-33, 52.
Consistent with Maryland la w, an Administrative
Law Judge (ALJ) held a hearing on April 11, 2023, and
determined that petitioner should be involuntarily admitted.  Pet.App.22a; Md. Code  Ann., Health-Gen. § 10-
632(e)(2).  Petitioner sought judicial review of the ALJ’s
decision.  Doe, 2025 WL 3553026, at *2.  Her father also
filed suit in Maryland state co urt, seeking judicial recognition of the purported advance directive.  J.A.6-7.
3.  Meanwhile, given petiti oner’s history of noncompliance with medication, petitioner’s care team at BWMC
recommended administering a long-lasting, injectable
form of the antipsychotic medication petitioner was already taking orally.  See J.A.20, 25-26, 177-79.  Petitioner
refused the medication, and consistent with Maryland law,
the hospital held two Clinical Review Panels.  Md. Code
Ann., Health-Gen. § 10-708(b)(2), (c)(1), (g); J.A.20, 22,

5

182.  Both panels approved administration of the injectable medication.  J.A.20, 22, 25.  However, the hospital
never administered the medication to petitioner.
Petitioner appealed the second panel’s decision to an
ALJ, who held a “de novo hearing” and affirmed the panel.
Md. Code Ann., Health-Gen. § 10-708(l)(6); J.A.26, 30.  Petitioner then appealed the ALJ’s finding to Maryland state
court on May 3, 2023.  J.A.7; Md. Code Ann., Health-Gen.
§ 10-708(m)(1).
4.  Notwithstanding three pending lawsuits—her father’s advance-directive lawsuit, her involuntaryadmission appeal, and her in voluntary-medication appeal—petitioner filed three additional lawsuits against
respondents in short order:  (1) a petition for a writ of habeas corpus filed in Maryland state court on May 5, 2023,
which resulted in the consent order at issue here, J.A.7;
(2) a petition for judicial rele ase, in which petitioner filed
three emergency motions for judicial release in Maryland
state court between May 28 an d June 6, 2023, J.A.7; and
(3) a due-process suit filed in federal district court on June
9, 2023, seeking damages and an injunction requiring petitioner’s discharge, see J.A.7; Pet.App.23a.  This set
brought petitioner to six lawsuits out of the eventual eight
she would file.
In the state-court habeas case, petitioner, her five attorneys (across three law firms), and respondents
negotiated a settlement agr eement, which set out petitioner’s safe discharge plan.  See Pet.App.24a.  Such
discharge plans are required under Maryland law.  Md.
Code Ann., Health-Gen. § 19-308 .8(c), (d).  Petitioner’s
counsel then asked the state court to enter the settlement
agreement as a consent order.  See Pet.App.24a.  The consent order provided that petitioner would obtain a new

6

psychiatrist, take her medication, and dismiss the pending
lawsuits.  J.A.159-61.
The court, counsel for resp ondents, and petitioner’s
five attorneys signed the cons ent order on June 12, 2023,
representing that they “approved [the order] as to form
and content.”  J.A.161-63 (capitalization omitted).  BWMC
then discharged petitioner.  No party has ever attempted
to enforce the consent order.
Petitioner’s five attorneys dismissed the federal dueprocess lawsuit with prejudic e on June 26, 2023, as required by the parties’ agreement.  See Pet.App.24a.  But
despite herself demanding entry of the consent order—
which secured her discharge—petitioner retained new
counsel and appealed the consent order to the Appellate
Court of Maryland on June 28, 2023.  Pet.App.24a-25a.
B. Procedural Background
1.  Meanwhile, on June 22, 2023, petitioner and the
same counsel who appealed the consent order initiated
this seventh lawsuit.  Petiti oner and her parents sued respondents UMMS, BWMC, tw o BWMC employees, and
others.  Pet.App.24a; J.A.1.  The complaint asked the district court to:
 “Declare that the ‘Consent Order’ violates the
Maryland Declaration of Rights and the Due
Process clause of th e Fourteenth Amendment
and is therefore unconstitutional, unenforceable, and void ab initio”;
 “Declare further that the ‘Consent Order’ is
also void and unenforceable because it was obtained under duress …”;

7

 “Grant preliminary and permanent injunctive
relief preventing enforcement of the ‘Consent
Order”; and
 Grant any other relief.
J.A.46.
The next day, petitioner moved for a temporary restraining order (TRO) “preve nting enforcement of the
Consent Order.”  D. Ct. Dkt. 6 at 7.  On June 26, 2023, the
district court ordered supplemental briefing on whether
petitioner’s challenge was properly in federal court and
the application of abstention principles.  D. Ct. Dkt. 10 at
1.  Following supplemental brie fing, the district court issued a letter order on August 23, 2023, concluding that the
collateral-attack doctrine, Younger abstention, and Colorado River abstention did not bar petitioner’s suit.  D. Ct.
Dkt. 27 at 2-5.
On September 5, 2023, the di strict court held a hearing on the TRO motion.  Addressing the merits, the court
observed that petitioner wa s “highly represented” in the
consent-order proceedings, with “five lawyers from three
different law firms.”  J.A.50, 71.  Those very same lawyers
dismissed the federal due-process case “with prejudice”—
behavior difficult to square with “truly believ[ing] your clients were under duress.”  J.A.64.  The court further
observed that accepting petitioner’s duress claim would
incentivize parties to settle, g et their side of the bargain,
“and then claim duress to try to keep [the other] side from
enforcing” the rest of the agreement.  See J.A.50.  The
court denied petitioner’s TRO motion at the hearing and
in an order filed that same day.  J.A.108; D. Ct. Dkt. 34.
2.  On October 23, 2023, UMMS respondents moved
to dismiss the case on the merits.  D. Ct. Dkt. 40.  About a

8

week later, on October 31, 2023, petitioner moved the Appellate Court of Maryland to stay her consent-order
appeal, citing the pendency  of the federal suit.
Pet.App.25a.  Petitioner’s stay motion claimed that the
state-court “matter [wa]s based on the same facts and
events at issue in [this federal-court case],” and sought to
“prevent inconsistent rulings.”  D. Ct. Dkt. 81-1 at 1.  The
Appellate Court of Maryland entered a stay on November
13, 2023, which has been extended and remains in effect.
See Pet.App.36a-37a.1
On July 23, 2024, the federal district court dismissed
the complaint based on Rooker-Feldman, which the court
raised sua sponte.2  Pet.App.26a, 35a.
3.  The Fourth Circuit a ffirmed.  Pet.App.2a.  The
court recognized “an uncanny resemblance” between petitioner’s case and Rooker.  Pet.App.7a.  Just like the
plaintiffs in Rooker, petitioner challenged a state-court
judgment in federal court, claimed the state-court judgment violated the Constitution, and asked a district court
to declare that state-court judgment “‘void’ and ‘unenforceable.’”  Pet.App.7a-8a (citation omitted).
Petitioner’s case also lack ed “the circumstances that
led the Supreme Court to hold that the Rooker-Feldman
doctrine did not apply in Exxon.”  Pet.App.8a.  Petitioner
filed her federal lawsuit after entry of the state-court consent judgment.  Pet.App.8a.  And petitioner was seeking
to “undo” the state-court consent judgment instead of just
 
1 Because respondents were already defending the federal-court litigation at that point and wished to  avoid the burdens of duplicative
litigation, respondents did not oppose petitioner’s stay motion.
2 The court dismissed petitioner’s parents’ claims for failure to state a
claim; the Fourth Circuit affirmed.  Pet.App.19a-20a.

9

“protect[ing]” herself from a state-court loss or seeking to
relitigate previously decided issues.  Pet.App.8a-9a (quoting Exxon, 544 U.S. at 293-94).
The Fourth Circuit also rejected petitioner’s argument that Rooker-Feldman did not apply because the
Maryland Supreme Court had not yet reviewed the judgment.  Pet.App.15a.  The cour t reasoned that Congress’
decision to withhold jurisdiction from the Supreme Court
over intermediary state-court decisions did not somehow
imbue district courts with jurisdiction over those decisions.  Pet.App.16a-17a.
At bottom, “this case [wa]s too much like Rooker to
justify a different result.”  Pet.App.2a.  Although “few
claims warrant dismissal under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine,” petitioner’s claims “fit the bill.”  Pet.App.20a.  The
court thus affirmed dismissal of T.M.’s claims, modifying
the dismissal to be without prejudice.  Pet.App.2a.
4.  While this case was still pending before the district
court, in December 2023 petiti oner filed yet another federal lawsuit against the UMMS-related respondents—her
eighth lawsuit.  23-3318 Compl.  Petitioner brought federal disability-discrimination claims and other state-law
claims seeking damages.  Id. ¶¶ 126-56.  The district court
dismissed the complaint on the merits, and the Fourth
Circuit recently affirmed.  Doe, 2025 WL 3553026, at *1.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
I.  Under Rooker-Feldman, federal district courts
lack jurisdiction to review and reject state-court judgments, whether or not those judgments are subject to
further state-court appellate review.
A.  Rooker-Feldman arises from bedrock jurisdictional principles.  First, federal courts enjoy only the
jurisdiction afforded to them  by Congress.  And second,

10

Congress has not vested lowe r federal courts with general-purpose appellate jurisdic tion to review and reject
state-court judgments.  Only this Court has appellate jurisdiction over state-court judgments.  Rooker-Feldman
recognizes that suits like peti tioner’s invoke appellate jurisdiction, which federal dist rict courts simply do not
possess.
B.  Petitioner does not dispute that her lawsuit meets
all four of Rooker-Feldman’s elements as articulated in
Exxon.  Petitioner (1) claims to be a “state-court loser[]”
who (2) sued in federal court (on June 22, 2023) after entry
of a state-court judgment (the consent order entered on
June 12, 2023), (3) she “complain[s] of injuries caused by”
that judgment, and (4) she asks  the district court to declare that judgment void.  See Exxon , 544 U.S. at 284.
Those principles suffice to resolve this case, as the courts
below held.
C.  Petitioner incorrectly contends that Rooker-Feldman contains a stealth fifth element—that Rooker-
Feldman applies only when the state-court judgment is no
longer subject to review in the state courts.
Exxon did not create that counterintuitive and anomalous rule.  Petitioner relies on stray language from
Exxon’s discussion of Rooker’s and Feldman’s procedural
histories.  But that is not the place this Court typically announces legal rules.  Petitioner ’s reliance on this Court’s
post-Exxon cases is similarly unavailing.  None supports
petitioner’s proposed rule.
Section 1257 does not help ei ther.  Petitioner argues
that Rooker-Feldman rests on a negative inference from
section 1257, meaning that district courts lack jurisdiction
only over those state-court judgments that this Court has

11

jurisdiction to review unde r 28 U.S.C. § 1257.  But petitioner’s proposed rule undermines her negative-inference
argument.  This Court canno t review state trial-court
judgments that were never a ppealed.  Yet, under petitioner’s proposed rule, beca use such judgments are not
“subject to further review in state court,” Pet. Br. I, 4-5,
15, 18-19, 28-30, 43, Rooker-Feldman blocks the suit.
Rooker-Feldman stems from more than a negative inference from section 1257.  Rooker-Feldman holds that
federal district-court review and rejection of state-court
judgments is an exercise of appellate jurisdiction—jurisdiction Congress has not gran ted lower federal courts.
Federal district courts do no t gain appellate jurisdiction
whenever this Court lacks it under section 1257.  It is
wholly implausible that Congress authorized this Court to
review state-court judgments only after affording state
appellate courts the opportunity to correct any error, but
permitted any one of the 94 fede ral district courts to review them as long as state appeals remained open.  As our
Nation’s unbroken history reflects, only this Court has authority to review and reject state-court judgments, unless
Congress specifically authorizes otherwise.
Petitioner also argues that Rooker-Feldman suits do
not invoke appellate jurisdiction at all and thus fall under
Congress’ grant of original juri sdiction to district courts
in section 1331.  That argument  is foreclosed by multiple
of this Court’s cases, it fa lls outside the question presented, and it is wrong to boot.  The same goes for
petitioner’s attempt to analogize Rooker-Feldman suits to
collateral attacks.
Nor can petitioner’s appeal to policy save her rule.
Petitioner claims that Rooker-Feldman confuses courts.
But her cited cases profess confusion about the review-

12

and-rejection element, not the question presented.  Moreover, petitioner’s approach  would require extensive
litigation over whether state-court proceedings are sufficiently final, a question that already vexes courts on her
side of the split.
D.  Petitioner’s rule would turn federalism and comity
principles on their head.  District-court appellate review
of state-court judgments sti ll subject to appeal in the
state-court system would be particularly offensive.  Under
petitioner’s rule, state-cour t losers who complete their
state-court appeals are barred from district-court litigation but state-court losers who jump into federal court are
not.  Petitioner pays lip service to this concern, but argues
that other doctrines, like ab stention and preclusion, will
stem the tide of state-court lo sers’ suits.  But the district
court held that many of those doctrines do not apply in this
case, leaving Rooker-Feldman with an essential role to
play in confining federal distri ct-court jurisdiction to its
congressionally intended scope.
II.  Petitioner’s request that this Court overrule
Rooker-Feldman is neither encompassed in the question
presented nor raised in the petition.  Petitioner urged this
Court to review one specific question about Rooker-Feldman’s application to a particular fact pattern.  The Court
should not entertain petitioner’s eleventh-hour attempt to
turn this case into a referendum on this Court’s centuryold precedent.
ARGUMENT
I. The District Court Lacked Jurisdiction over Petitioner’s
Suit
Federal district courts lack jurisdiction to adjudicate
“cases brought by state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments rendered before the

13

district court proceedings commenced and inviting district
court review and rejectio n of those judgments.”  Exxon,
544 U.S. at 284.  This is such  a case, and petitioner does
not argue to the contrary.  Instead, petitioner urges the
Court to add a new element to Rooker-Feldman, contending that it should not apply if the state-court judgment
“remains subject to further re view in state court.”  Pet.
Br. 15.  Neither Exxon, nor section 1257, nor section 1331
supports that limitation.  And petitioner does not persuasively explain away the massi ve federalism and comity
implications of her rule.
A. Federal District Courts Do Not Have Appellate Jurisdiction to Review State-Court Judgments
1.  Rooker-Feldman “is not so much a ‘doctrine’ as a
basic fact of federal statutory law.”  Reed v. Goertz , 598
U.S. 230, 244-45 (2023) (Thomas, J., dissenting).  “Federal
courts … are courts of limited jurisdiction.”  Royal Canin
U. S. A., Inc. v. Wullschleger, 604 U.S. 22, 26 (2025) (quoting Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am. , 511 U.S.
375, 377 (1994)).  “They possess  only that power authorized by Constitution and statute.”  Kokkonen, 511 U.S. at
377.  “Congress determines, through its grants of jurisdiction, which suits those courts can resolve.”  Royal Canin,
604 U.S. at 26.
Congress’ grants of jurisdiction—and their attendant
limitations—reflect its “decision to implement[] a dual
system of federal and state courts.”  Chick Kam Choo v.
Exxon Corp., 486 U.S. 140, 146 (1988).  “[F]rom the beginning we have had in this country two essentially separate
legal systems,” each of which “proceeds independently of
the other with ultimate review in this Court of the federal
questions raised in either system.”  Atl. Coast Line R. Co.
v. Bhd. of Locomotive Eng’rs, 398 U.S. 281, 286 (1970).

14

In granting federal courts jurisdiction, both the
Framers and Congress carefully distinguished between
original and appellate jurisdiction.  “‘[T]he essential criterion of appellate jurisdiction ’ … is ‘that it revises and
corrects the proceedings in a cause already instituted.’”
Ortiz v. United States , 585 U.S. 427, 436 (2018) (quoting
Marbury v. Madison, 5 U.S. (1 Cranch) 137, 175 (1803)).
In other words, suits “for the purpose of revising [another
court’s] decision” invoke “appellate” jurisdiction.  Ex
parte Bollman, 8 U.S. (4 Cranch) 75, 86 (1807) (Marshall,
C.J.); see also Reed , 598 U.S. at 243-44 (Thomas, J. dissenting) (“the criterion which distinguishes appellate from
original jurisdiction, is that it revises and corrects the decisions of another tribunal” (cleaned up)).  Thus, “a case or
controversy is appellate in nature when the relief-seeking
party’s injury is traceable to  the allegedly erroneous action of another court and re quires a remedy correcting
that judicial action ( e.g., reversal or vacatur of the challenged judgment).”  Reed, 598 U.S. at 244 (Thomas, J.
dissenting) (emphasis omitted).
Congress granted only this  Court appellate jurisdiction to “review[]” and correct certain “[f]inal judgments or
decrees rendered by the highest court of a State in which
a decision could be had.”  28 U.S.C. § 1257.  District courts,
however, “have not been given such powers.”  Atl. Coast
Line, 398 U.S. at 286.  Congress instead endowed district
courts only with “original jurisdiction” over specific types
of actions.  See, e.g., 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330,  1331, 1332, 1333,
1343.  Thus, while district courts have “virtually unflagging obligation … to exercise the jurisdiction given them,”
Colo. River Water Conserva tion Dist. v. United States ,
424 U.S. 800, 817 (1976), “the converse also holds true,” see
FBI v. Fikre, 601 U.S. 234, 240 (2024).  District courts may
not exercise jurisdiction they do not possess in the first
place.

15

2.  Rooker-Feldman proceeds from these basic principles.
In Rooker, the plaintiffs sued a trust company, claiming it breached a trust agreement covering a trust in lands.
Rooker v. Fid. Tr. Co., 131 N.E. 769, 770 (Ind. 1921).  After
the trust company prevailed in the state courts, the plaintiffs turned to federal court.  Rooker, 263 U.S. at 414-15.
The Rooker plaintiffs brought a bill in equity, which was
an original suit asking a fede ral district court to declare
that state-court judgment “null and void” and “rendered
and affirmed” in violation of the Constitution.  Id.
A unanimous Court held that the plaintiffs’ suit did
not belong in federal district  court because it sought the
exercise of appellate jurisdicti on over a state-court judgment.  “Under the legislation of Congress, no court of the
United States other than this court could entertain a proceeding to reverse or modify the judgment fo r errors of
that character.”  Id. at 416.  Distinguishing between “original” and “appellate” jurisdiction, the Court observed that
the plaintiffs’ suit would require “an exercise of appellate
jurisdiction,” but “[t]he jurisdiction possessed by the District Courts is strictly original.”  Id.  Thus, the suit was
“not within the District Court’s jurisdiction as defined by
Congress.”  Id. at 415.
This Court added that “[i] f the constitutional questions stated in the bill actua lly arose in the cause, it was
the province and duty of the state courts to decide them.”
Id.  And “[i]f the decision was wrong, that did not make
the judgment void, but merely left it open to reversal or
modification in an appropriate and timely appellate proceeding.”  Id.  The Court thus saw the bill in equity for
what it was:  “an attempt to  get rid of the judgment for
alleged errors of law committed  in the exercise of [the
state court’s] jurisdiction.”  Id. at 416.

16

This Court reaffirmed that principle in Feldman.
That case involved a District  of Columbia rule that required individuals to grad uate from an approved law
school before admission to th e bar.  460 U.S. at 455-56.
The D.C. Court of Appeals de nied waivers to two applicants; they sued in federal district court, claiming that the
denials violated federal law and requesting injunctions
permitting them to sit for th e bar examination or, in one
case, to gain immediate bar admission.  Id. at 468-69, 472-
73.
This Court held that the district court had jurisdiction
to consider “a general challe nge to the constitutionality”
of the rule, but lacked jurisdiction to review the waiver denials by the state court in the applicants’ particular cases.
Id. at 482-83.  Those denials were “final determinations of
the District of Columbia Cour t of Appeals in judicial proceedings,” and “[r]eview of such determinations can be
obtained only in this Court.”  See id. at 476.  The Court
thus rejected the notion that  state-court orders concerning bar admission “may be reviewed … by … a lower
federal court.”  See id. at 483 n.16 (citation omitted).
After Feldman, some lower federa l courts began to
extend Rooker-Feldman “far beyond the contours of the
Rooker and Feldman cases.”  Exxon, 544 U.S. at 283.  This
Court ordered a course correction in Exxon.
Exxon involved parallel litigation.  Saudi Basic Industries sued ExxonMobil subsid iaries in Delaware state
court for a declaratory judg ment that certain royalty
charges were proper under their agreement.  Id. at 289.

C. Petitioner’s Proposed Rule Lacks Merit
Petitioner urges the Court to add a fifth element to
the test articulated in Exxon:  that the state-court judgment is not “subject to further review in state court.”  Pet.
Br. I, 4-5, 15, 18-19, 28-30, 43.  That limitation finds no support in this Court’s precedent, statutory authority, or

1. Exxon did not limit Rooker-Feldman to suits challenging state-court judgments not subject to further
review in state court
Petitioner (at 27) contends that Exxon “strongly suggests that Rooker-Feldman should not apply to cases filed
in federal court while proceedings in state court remain
pending.”  That is incorrect.
Look no further than Exxon’s express holding,
which—as just discussed, supra p. 17—identified four requirements without mentioni ng petitioner’s proposed
rule.  Petitioner (at 27) brus hes off the four enumerated
elements as “separate language in the introduction of the
opinion [that] did not contain an express finality limitation.”  But that “separate language” began with “The
Rooker-Feldman doctrine, we hold today,” 544 U.S. at 284
(emphasis added), which is a compelling signal that the
four-pronged rule statement that follows is Exxon’s holding.
Petitioner (at 26-27) attempts to derive her “finality”
rule from the Court’s recitation, seven pages later, of

20

Rooker’s and Feldman’s procedural histories, where the
Court noted that the federal suits in those cases came “after the state proceedings ended.”  See id. at 291.  But, as
the Fourth Circuit concluded, that summary of the procedural history did not create a “stealth fifth requirement

Court to overturn an injurious state-court judgment,” 544
U.S. at 281—a description that fits petitioner’s suit to a
tee.
More telling than Exxon’s recitation of Rooker’s and
Feldman’s procedural history is what Exxon said about
those cases’ reasoning and holdings.  Exxon explained
that Rooker “clarified [that] Congress had empowered
only this Court to exercise appellate authority to reverse
or modify a state-court judgment.”  Id. at 284 (citation
omitted).  The Court did not mention the unavailability of
further state-court appellate review.
The Court also echoed Feldman’s observation that
lower federal courts “lack[] authority to review a final judicial determination of the D.C. high court.”  Id.  T h e
“crucial question” in Feldman was not whether the “D.C.
high court” issued the judgment  (a fact no one disputed),
but whether the “final … determination” was “judicial in
nature.”  Id. at 285 (citation omitted).  The fact that the
D.C. high court, as opposed to the D.C. superior court, issued the decision was of no moment.
Nor does Exxon’s explanation of Rooker-Feldman’s
rationale turn on the fact th at those federal suits were
brought after the conclusion of state-court proceedings.
See supra pp. 15-17.  Instead, the Court explained that the
federal actions in Rooker and Feldman were “out of

21

bounds” because they “essentially invited federal courts of
first instance to review an d reverse unfavorable statecourt judgments,” which would involve the exercise of “appellate,” rather than “original,” jurisdiction.  Exxon, 544
U.S. at 283-84.  That is true regardless of which state court
rendered the judgment.
Petitioner (at 19, 26) points out that Exxon observed
that “ Rooker and Feldman exhibit the limited circumstances in which this Court’s appellate jurisdiction over
state-court judgments … prec ludes a United States district court from exercising su bject-matter jurisdiction in
an action it would otherwise be empowered to adjudicate
under a congressional grant of authority.”  Id. at 291.  But
the Court immediately clarified what it meant, explaining
that “[t]he Rooker-Feldman doctrine merely recognizes
that 28 U.S.C. § 1331 is a grant of original jurisdiction, and
does not authorize district courts to exercise appellate jurisdiction over state-court judgments, which Congress has
reserved to this Court” under section 1257(a).  Id at 292.
(citation omitted).  Thus, Exxon explained that (1) district
courts lack an affirmative gran t of jurisdiction to review
state-court judgments and (2 ) section 1257, which “vests
authority to review a state court’s judgment solely in this
Court,” buttresses that conclusion.  Id. at 291-92.
While petitioner (at 27) contends that Exxon sought
to “return the doctrine to its narrow foundations,”
Exxon’s concerns about Rooker-Feldman’s scope had
nothing to do with its applic ability to potentially appealable state-court judgments.  The Court’s concern was with
Rooker-Feldman’s application to preclude federal suits
that do not challenge a sta te-court judgment because the
federal suit was filed before the state court rendered any
judgment at all—i.e., parallel federal suits.  Those suits by

22

definition do not trigger the exercise of appellate jurisdiction.  As the Court explained, “the Third Circuit
misperceived the narrow ground occupied by Rooker-
Feldman” because “ExxonMobil plainly has not repaired
to federal court to undo the Delaware judgment in its favor,” given that it sued before any such judgment existed.
Id. at 284, 293-94.
Petitioner (at 36) also references post- Exxon cases
that she claims have “continued to define [ Rooker-Feldman’s] scope narrowly.”  But none purports to limit
Rooker-Feldman to judgments issued by a State’s highest
or supreme court.  Some of the cases she cites instead describe Rooker-Feldman as “prohibit[ing] federal courts
from adjudicating cases brought by state-court losing parties challenging state-court judgments” and as confined to

review and rejection of the state court’s judgments.”  Reed
v. Goertz, 598 U.S. 230, 235 (2023) (first quote); Skinner v.
Switzer, 562 U.S. 521, 532 (2011) (second quote) (cleaned
up).  Those descriptions accurately capture Rooker-Feldman’s narrow scope, into which petitioner’s case falls.
Other cases that petitioner (at 36) cites state that under Rooker-Feldman “lower federal courts are precluded
from exercising appellate juri sdiction over final statecourt judgments.”  Lance v. Dennis , 546 U.S. 459, 463
(2006); see also Stop the Beach Renourishment, Inc. v.
Florida Dep’t of Env’t Prot., 560 U.S. 702, 727 (2010) (“final state-court judgments”).  Those cases likewise do not
suggest that only decisions by  a state high court trigger
Rooker-Feldman.  Although petitioner repeatedly
equates “final” state-court decisions with decisions that
are not “subject to further review in state court” ( e.g., at
28), the two are not necessarily the same.  State trial

23

§ 1291 (“The courts of appeals … shall have jurisdiction of
appeals from all final decisions of the district courts.”).
Notably, for this Court to review a state-court decision under section 1257, the decision must be both “final” and
“rendered by the highest court of a State in which a decision could be had.”
Petitioner’s reliance on language describing Rooker-
Feldman as applying in cases involving decisions by
“highest state court[s]” is similarly misplaced.  See Pet.
Br. 31 (citing ASARCO Inc. v. Kadish , 490 U.S. 605, 622
(1989) and Skinner, 562 U.S. at 531).  The language from
Skinner that petitioner highlights merely describes the
facts of Rooker and Feldman.  See 562 U.S. at 531.  And
ASARCO involved the question whether the petitioner

by Arizona’s highest court, and the Court was merely describing how Rooker-Feldman would apply to the facts

2. Section 1257 does not support petitioner’s rule
Petitioner (at 28-32) contends that Rooker-Feldman
rests solely on a negative implication from 28 U.S.C.
§ 1257, which grants this Cour t jurisdiction over only
“[f]inal judgments or decrees  rendered by the highest
court of a State in which a decision could be had.”  Thus,
her argument goes, Rooker-Feldman does not apply to
cases that fall outside section 1257’s ambit—i.e., “cases in
which the state-court judgment remains subject to further
review in state court.”  Pet. Br. I, 4-5, 15-16, 18-19, 28-30,
43.
a.  Petitioner’s logic fails right out of the gate.  Section
1257 applies only to judgments that have reached a State’s

24

highest court.  Thus, this Court may not review lower state
trial- or appellate-court judgments that become unreviewable by the State’s highes t court because an appeal
deadline has expired.  But under petitioner’s rule, Rooker-
Feldman still forecloses federal-court appellate review of
such judgments because they are not “subject to further
review in state court.”
Indeed, several circuits petitioner embraces, Pet. 15-
17, hold that Rooker-Feldman applies so long as the time
for state-court appeal has expired.  See, e.g., Federación
de Maestros de P.R. v. Junt a de Relaciones del Trabajo
de P.R., 410 F.3d 17, 24 (1st Cir. 2005) (state proceedings
end when “the time for appeal … exipire[s]”); Malhan v.
Sec’y U.S. Dep’t of State , 938 F.3d 453, 459-60 (3d Cir.
2019) (same).  Petitioner’s rule produces strange and
anomalous results:  federal courts would have jurisdiction
to review a state trial court’ s judgment if the state-court
loser files the day before the deadline for noticing an appeal expires, but federal courts would  not  have
jurisdiction if the party files one day after the deadline
passes.
b.  Even putting the faulty logic aside, petitioner misperceives Rooker-Feldman’s doctrinal underpinning.
Petitioner (at 16, 19-20, 28-29) repeatedly depicts Rooker-
Feldman as solely “rest[ing] on a negative inference from
the Court’s grant of appellate jurisdiction in 28 U.S.C.
§ 1257.”  Based on that premise, petitioner reasons that if
section 1257 does not grant this Court authority to review
a given state-court judgment (because state-court appellate review has not yet been exhausted), then Rooker-
Feldman does not bar federal district courts from adjudicating cases challenging that judgment.
But Rooker-Feldman goes deeper than section 1257.
Rooker-Feldman “recognizes that 28 U.S.C. § 1331 is a

25

grant of original jurisdiction, and does not authorize district courts to exercise appe llate jurisdiction over statecourt judgments, which Congress has reserved to this
Court.”  Exxon, 544 U.S. at 292 (quoting Verizon Md. Inc.
v. Pub. Serv. Comm’n of Md., 535 U.S. 635, 644 n.3 (2002)).
In other words, Rooker-Feldman recognizes that federal
district courts cannot “enter tain a proceeding to reverse
or modify” a state-court judgment because “[t]o do so
would be an exercise of appellate jurisdiction,” while
“[t]he jurisdiction possessed by the District Courts is
strictly original.”  Rooker, 263 U.S. at 416.  “Thus, if the
losing party in a state judicial proceeding claims that the
state judgment itself violates his federal rights” that is “a
claim that calls for an exercise of appellate jurisdiction”
and “[h]e may not seek” such review “under the guise of
an original action in federal district court.”  Reed, 598 U.S.
at 245 (Thomas, J., dissenting) (cleaned up).
Feldman directly forecloses petitioner’s argument.
Feldman confronted the Fifth Circuit’s reasoning that a
“limit on [this Court’s] certiorari jurisdiction” means “that
a federal district court has ju risdiction.”  460 U.S. at 482
n.16.  (There, the alleged limi t at issue was this Court’s
potential lack of “jurisdiction” to review state-court judgments when the petitioner failed to raise the federal
constitutional issue in state court.  Id.)  This Court explained:  That “reasoning … is flawed” because “lower
federal courts possess no powe r whatever to sit in direct
review of state court decisions.”  Id. (quoting Atl. Coast
Line, 398 U.S. at 296).  “[T]hat [this Court] may not have
jurisdiction to review a final state court judgment because
of a petitioner’s failure to raise his constitutional claims in
state court does not mean that  a United States District
Court should have jurisdiction over the claims.”  Id.

26

Petitioner offers no logica l rationale for construing
section 1257’s grant of appellate jurisdiction to this Court
over some cases implicitly to permit  district courts to exercise appellate jurisdiction over other cases.  That a statecourt judgment remains susceptible to further state-court
review makes federal district-court intervention less appropriate, not more.  Petiti oner’s contrary rule is
downright bizarre.
After all, when it comes to federal-court intervention
to “upset the decision of a State court,” “we are in the
realm of potential conflict between the courts of two different governments.”  Radio Station WOW, Inc. v.
Johnson, 326 U.S. 120, 124 (1945).  It is for that reason
that “ever since 1789, Congress has granted this Court the
power to intervene in State litigation only after the highest court of a State in which a decision in the suit could be
had has rendered a final judgment or decree.”  Id. (citation
omitted); Republic Nat. Gas Co. v. Oklahoma, 334 U.S. 62,
67 (1948).  If that constraint “is an important factor in the
smooth working of our federal system” when it comes to
Supreme Court review of state-court judgments, Radio
Station WOW, 326 U.S. at 124, it makes little sense that
federal district courts wou ld be able to intervene midstream.  It cannot be, as petitioner would have it, that the
Rooker plaintiffs’ only mistake was pursuing orderly appeals through the state-court system before turning to
federal court, when instead they should have asked a federal district court to jump in partway through.
Congress authorized only this Court to review statecourt judgments, and even then only after waiting for the
state appellate process to play out.  As this Court has recognized, shortly after the Founding, when section 1257
was enacted, Congress’ “general policy” was that statecourt proceedings “should normally be allowed to continue

27

unimpaired by intervention of the lower federal courts,
with relief from error, if any, through the state appellate
courts and ultimately this Court.”  Chick Kam Choo, 486
U.S. at 146 (citation omitted).  Petitioner’s rule would upset the Nation’s centuries-long practice.
3. Rooker-Feldman suits do not invoke original jurisdiction
Petitioner (at 32-35) argues that federal-court review
and rejection of state-court judgments involves original,
rather than appellate, jurisdiction.  But that argument requires overruling Rooker-Feldman and is not presented.
In any event, her argument that Rooker-Feldman suits fit
within section 1331’s grant of original jurisdiction is wrong
and her analogy to collateral attacks is inapt.
a.  Petitioner’s argument is foreclosed and not presented.  Petitioner’s argument immediately runs
headlong into a wall of precedent, as petitioner herself (at
33-34) recognizes.  This Cour t has repeatedly described
requests for federal courts to declare state-court judgments “void”—like petitioner sought here—as requiring
the exercise of appellate jurisdiction.  See supra pp. 24-25;
Rooker, 263 U.S. at 416; Exxon, 544 U.S. at 292; Verizon
Md., 535 U.S. at 644 n.3.  And as the decision below found,
petitioner’s federal case inherently seeks review and rejection of the state-court consent order— i.e., the very
same relief sought in both Rooker and Feldman, see supra
pp. 18-19.
Moreover, this case does not present the question
whether suits seeking review and rejection of state-court
judgments invoke appellate jurisdiction.  This Court has
already held that they do, and the petition did not challenge those holdings.  The p etition instead argued that
Rooker-Feldman does not apply when further state-court

28

review remains possible.  See infra pp. 43-45.  Petitioner’s
new argument amounts to an unpreserved challenge to a
century of Rooker-Feldman cases.
b.  Section 1331 does not authorize federal courts to
review and reject state-court judgments.   In all events,
petitioner (at 32) is wrong that her suit falls within section
1331 because she purportedly brought a freestanding
cause of action under 42 U.S. C. § 1983.  Courts exercise
appellate jurisdiction when they “revise[] and correct[]
the proceedings in a cause already instituted.”  Ortiz, 585
U.S. at 436 (quoting Marbury, 5 U.S. (1 Cranch) at 175);
supra p. 14.  Petitioner’s federal suit asks the district court
to intervene and “[d]eclare … void and unenforceable,” including on grounds of dure ss, J.A.46, th e state-court
consent order issued in “proceedings in a cause already
instituted” in Maryland state court, see Ortiz, 585 U.S. at
436 (citation omitted).  And because Maryland courts permit appeals of consent orders  only upon a showing of
duress, see infra p. 37, her state-court appeal and her district-court suit seek to invalidate the consent order on the
same exact basis.  Petitioner’s  suit, and others like it, involve appellate jurisdiction.
Of course petitioner did no t style her federal suit as
an appeal, but only because no formal mechanism exists
for directly appealing a state- court judgment to a federal
district court.  See, e.g., Atl. Coast Line , 398 U.S. at 286.
Rooker, however, made clear that “an aggrieved litigant
cannot be permitted to do indirectly what he no longer can
do directly.”  263 U.S. at 416.   Plaintiffs “may not ‘see[k]
what in substance would be appellate review of the state
judgment’ under the guise of an  original action in federal
district court.”  Reed, 598 U.S. at 245 (Thomas, J., dissenting) (quoting Johnson v. De Grandy , 512 U.S. 997, 1005-
06 (1994)).  Plaintiffs cannot simply “leave[] off the ‘appeal’

29

heading, but nevertheless ask[ ] the federal court to reverse, nullify, or enjoin the execution of a state court civil
judgment.”  Suzanna Sherry, Judicial Federalism in the
Trenches: The Rooker-Feldman Doctrine in Action , 74
Notre Dame L. Rev. 1085, 1091 (1999).
Worse, petitioner offers no reason why her reading of
section 1331 would not apply to section 1332 as well, given
that both statutes use the term “original jurisdiction.”  See
Pet. Br. 6.  Thus, in cases involving complete diversity, petitioner’s rule would allow fe deral courts to review and
reject state-court judgments based only on state law, even
before state appellate courts have weighed in.  Congress
surely did not intend either section 1331 or section 1332 to
effect such a massive intrusion on state sovereignty.  See
infra pp. 39-42.
Petitioner’s interpretation of section 1331 as permitting federal district courts to review and reject civil statecourt judgments runs contra ry to Congress’ centurieslong historical practice.  When Congress wants to empower federal courts to interfere with state-court
proceedings, it says so “explicitly” and includes guardrails.  Exxon, 544 U.S. at 292 n.8.
Take Congress’ grant of appellate jurisdiction to this
Court in section 1257 to revi ew state-court judgments.
That statute contains careful finality limitations and permits this Court to step in only once the state’s highest
court has had a chance to revise  any errors itself.  It is
implausible that Congress authorized district courts to do
the same without any similar constraints.
Consider three other statutes in which Congress provided a “clear statement” authorizing federal courts to
interfere with state-court proceedings.  Cf. United States
v. Bass, 404 U.S. 336, 349 (1971); Gregory v. Ashcroft, 501

30

U.S. 452, 460-61, 470 (1991).  First, since the creation of
the federal-court system, Congress empowered lower
courts to accept “petition[s] for the removal of the cause
for trial” from state court to federal court in particular
classes of cases.  Judiciary Act of 1789, ch. 20, § 12, 1 Stat.
73, 79.  That power has expanded over time, but it has always had a basis in statute.  See 28 U.S.C. § 1441.  And
Congress has always imposed limitations on removal, such
a s  t i m e  l i m i t s  o n  f i l i n g  n o t i c e s  o f  r e m o v a l .   E.g., id.
§ 1446(b)(1) (30 days after service of complaint); Judiciary
Act of 1789, ch. 20, § 12, 1 Stat. 73, 79 (“at the time of entering [the] appearance in such state court”).  Petitioner’s
approach blows by these carefu l statutory restrictions on
removal by allowing state-cour t defendants to take their
chances in state court but then, if they lose, file an original
action in federal court challenging a state-court judgment
so long as the state appellate process remains ongoing.
Second, the writ of habeas co rpus provides another
avenue for federal-court interference, but this too has always been grounded in specific statutory text.  See Ex
parte Bollman, 8 U.S. at 93-94.  The Judiciary Act of 1789
granted lower courts the power to issue habeas petitions
for federal prisoners.  Judiciary Act of 1789, ch. 20, § 14, 1
Stat. 73, 81-82.  For decades, federal courts could not provide habeas relief to state prisoners.  E.g., Ex parte Dorr,
44 U.S. (3 How.) 103, 105 (1845); see Felker v. Turpin, 518
U.S. 651, 659-60 (1996) (noting three narrow statutory exceptions).
The Habeas Corpus Act of  1867 finally endowed federal courts with “power to grant writs of habeas corpus in
all cases where any person may be restrained.”  Habeas
Corpus Act of 1867, chs. 27-28,  14 Stat. 385.  Today, district courts may entertain ha beas applications by “a
person in custody pursuant to the judgment of a State

31

court” under specific circumstances.  28 U.S.C. § 2254(a);
see also id. § 2241(a).  Like removal, the habeas power has
also been carefully limited.  Habeas actions have long involved an exhaustion requirement “as a matter of comity,”
even before the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act codified the requirement.  Wainwright v. Sykes,
433 U.S. 72, 80 (1977) (citing  Ex parte Royall , 117 U.S.
241, 253 (1886) and 28 U.S.C. § 2254).

to “foster care placement or termination of parental
rights” for Indian children th at violate federal law.  25
U.S.C. § 1914.  Petitioner’s read of section 1331 would render section 1914 superfluous, since, according to
petitioner, section 1331 alread y gives federal district
courts broad authority to “invalidate” state-court orders.
At the same time, Congress has enacted explicit
guardrails to prevent furthe r federal interference with
state proceedings.  For example, the Anti-Injunction Act,
which originates in the Judiciary Act of 1793, precludes
federal courts from staying state proceedings except under specific circumstances.  Act of Mar. 2, 1793, ch. 22, § 5,
1 Stat. 333, 334-35; 28 U.S.C. § 2283.
Petitioner’s amicus, for its part, identifies the Civil
Rights Acts, the Freedmen’s Bureau Act, and 42 U.S.C.
§ 1983 as evidence of Congress ’ post-Civil War desire to
allow broad federal-court interference with state proceedings, and argues that section 1331 should be interpreted
broadly in light of these statutes.  Constitutional Accountability Center Br. 2-3, 9-11.  But, at most, these statutes
show that Congress intended to  give plaintiffs a federal
forum to bring constitutional  claims against state actors.  Nothing in these stat utes suggests that Congress

32

wanted to empower federal dist rict courts to review and
reject state-court judgments.
Moreover, Congress had the blueprint for authorizing
such appellate review via se ction 1257, which dates back
to the Judiciary Act of 1789.  Congress could have drafted
any of these post-Civil War statutes—or section 1331—
similarly, but it did not.  Or Congress could have authorized lower federal-court revi ew of state civil judgments
when it expanded habeas relief for state prisoners in the
post-Civil War era.  Supra pp. 30-31.  But Congress did
nothing of the sort.
c.  Petitioner’s analogy to collateral attacks is unpersuasive.  Petitioner’s argument (at 32-33) that Rooker-
Feldman suits are akin to collateral attacks and therefore
invoke only original jurisdiction also fails.

Feldman, which argued that the Co urt “fail[ed] to distinguish between … appellate review and collateral attack,”
and that the Feldman plaintiffs’ suit involved only the latter.  460 U.S. at 490 (Stevens, J., dissenting).  But the

at 486 (majority op.).  Such su its could “only” be brought

1331 to collaterally attack st ate-court judgments.  Her

409, 444 (1897) (cited at Pet. Br. 33), and Earle v. McVeigh,

33

91 U.S. 503, 507 (1876) (same), held that state-court judgments were void because the state courts lacked
jurisdiction to enter the orders.  But neither case involved
a federal suit directly challenging a state-court judgment,
like petitioner’s suit here.  Instead, both cases arose out of
state-court enforcement actions, and the prior judgment’s

Earle, 91 U.S. at 506.
Griffith v. Bank of New York , 147 F.2d 899 (2d Cir.

federal courts to enjoin state-court judgments obtained by
fraud.  Id. at 901.  The case did not discuss subject-matter
jurisdiction.  Griffith’s holding is questionable, as  this
Court has observed that the Anti-Injunction Act renders
“very doubtful” the “foundatio n” of cases where “federal
courts have enjoined litiga nts from enforcing judgments
fraudulently obtained in the state courts.”  See Toucey v.
New York Life Ins. Co. , 314 U.S. 118, 136 (1941), superseded by statute as recognized  in Parsons Steel, Inc. v.
First Ala. Bank , 474 U.S. 518, 524 (1986).  The Restatement provision petitioner (at 33 n.4) cites likewise does not

aside a judgment.  See Restatement (Second) of Judgments § 70 (1982).
In any event, petitioner’s suit is not a collateral attack
a t  a l l .   H e r  s u i t  a s k s  t h e  d i s t r i c t  c o u r t  t o  d o  m o r e  t h a n
merely—as she puts it (at 32)—“prevent the enforcement

judgment is “incidental” to the new action.  See Restatement (Second) of Judgments ch. 5, intro. note b. (1982);

34

Restatement (First) of Judgments § 11 cmt. a (1942).  The
whole point of petitioner’s suit is to nullify the state-court
judgment.
Finally, petitioner (at 33) po ints to language indicating that federal-district-cou rt habeas jurisdiction has
“generally been deemed original.”  Pet. Br. 33 (quoting

Kholi, 562 U.S. 545, 552 (2011) and  United States v. Addonizio, 442 U.S. 178, 184 (1979)).  But see  Ex parte
Bollman, 8 U.S. at 101 (holding that this Court’s jurisdiction over direct habeas petitions is “clearly appellate”).
But this Court’s statements in “the unique context of habeas,” Jennings v. Stephens , 574 U.S. 271, 290 (2015)
(Thomas, J., dissenting), say nothing about the type of jurisdiction implicated by suit s seeking to undo state-court
civil judgments.
This Court already distinguished the jurisdictional
bases for habeas actions from Rooker-Feldman suits.  In
Exxon, the Court explained that while Congress “explicitly empower[ed] district cour ts to oversee certain statecourt judgments … in authorizing federal habeas review
of state prisoners’ petitions, ” section 1331 is a “grant of
original jurisdiction, and does not authorize district courts
to exercise appellate jurisdic tion over state-court judgments,” Exxon, 544 U.S. at 292 & n.8 (citation omitted);
see supra pp. 30-31.
Regardless, habeas suits are materially different
from Rooker-Feldman suits.  Historically, the writ allowed only a “limited” “attack  upon detention” when the
confining court lacked jurisdiction, Preiser v. Rodriguez ,
411 U.S. 475, 485 (1973), not a challenge to jurisdictionally
valid state-court judgments.  The writ could not be used to
relitigate and reject a considered state-court judgment

where the prisoner “had b een given an adequate opportunity to obtain full and fair  consideration of his federal
claim in the state courts.”  Wright v. West , 505 U.S. 277,
285 (1992) (opinion of Thomas, J.) (citation omitted).  “In
other words, the state-court judgment was entitled to absolute respect.”  Id. (cleaned up).
Even today, habeas petitions target the state-executive-branch’s detention, not invalidation of the state-court
judgment, as Rooker-Feldman suits like  petitioner’s do.
The writ’s basic purpose is to  “effect discharge from any
confinement contrary to the Constitution or fundamental
law.”  Preiser, 411 U.S. at 485.  Indeed, habeas petitions
often do not challenge state-co urt judgments at all.  For
instance, this Court has described “core” habeas actions

judgment.  But this Court co unsels that jurisdictional
rules should be “inflexible and without exception,” id. (citation omitted), not malleable and subject to

Rooker-Feldman applies to state-court judgments, regardless of whether those judgments are subject to

D. Petitioner’s Rule Would Undermine Federalism
and Finality While Encouraging Vexatious Litigation
The practical consequences of petitioner’s rule would
be astounding.  Any aggrieve d litigant could litigate in
state court, receive an adve rse state-court judgment, file
a federal suit asking a federal court to void that state-court
judgment, and appeal that state-court judgment to a state
appellate court as well.  Then, as petitioner acknowledges,
the federal district court wou ld “exercise[e] what ‘in substance’ would be appellate review.”  Pet. Br. 34 (citation
omitted).
In practice, therefore, petitioner’s rule would explode
the costs of defending against vexatious litigants, burdening two court systems along the way.  Petitioner’s
approach would be a boon for “litigants who, in the words
of judges who must deal with them, ‘refuse to accept adverse decisions’ and ‘repeatedly’ subject the courts to
‘vexatious and unmeritoriou s litigation.’”  Sherry, supra,
at 1086 (citation and footnote omitted).  The resulting system would be highly inefficient, imposing increased (and
unnecessary) costs on federal district courts.
Worse, petitioner’s rule produces nothing less than a
profound affront to federalism.  This country’s “dual system” of state and federal courts “could not function if state
and federal courts were free to fight each other for control
of a particular case.”  Atl. Coast Line , 398 U.S. at 286.
“Prevention of frequent federal court intervention is important to make the dual system work effectively.”  Chick
Kam Choo, 486 U.S. at 146.  “Cooperation and comity, not
competition and conflict, are essential to the federal design.”  Ruhrgas AG v. Marathon Oil Co., 526 U.S. 574, 586
(1999).  For centuries, ther efore, Congress has limited
federal-court interference with state courts, granting only

40

specific, constrained authority to oversee state-court
judgments.  Supra pp. 28-32.
Petitioner, however, would have federal courts supervise state-court judgments whenever the state-court loser
raises a federal question or the state-court parties have
diverse citizenship.  “State courts, like federal courts, have
a constitutional obligation to  safeguard personal liberties
and to uphold federal law.”  Stone v. Powell, 428 U.S. 465,
494 n.35 (1976) (citing Martin v. Hunter’s Lessee , 1 U.S.
(1 Wheat.) 304, 341-44 (1816)); see Rooker, 263 U.S. at 415.
They should be trusted to do their jobs without constant
supervision by federal district  courts.  And the affront to
state courts is particularly galling where, as here, the
plaintiff chose the state forum in the first place.
As now-Judge Rushing has explained, it is precisely
in these circumstances—when “a federal suit … seek[s]
what is essentially review of a state judgment while state
appeals are still pending”—that Rooker-Feldman safeguards federalism, promotes comity, and “prevent[s] the
inappropriate federal appeal of the state court judgment.”
Allison B. Jones, The Rooker-Feldman Doctrine: What
Does It Mean to Be Inextricably Intertwined? , 56 Duke
L.J. 643, 655-56 (2006); see Sherry, supra, at 1092-93
(deeming Rooker-Feldman “necessary and appropriate”
when “appeals are still pending”).
Petitioner (at 40-43) does not dispute that federalcourt review and rejection of state-court judgments raises
serious federalism concerns.  Instead, petitioner (at 40)
contends that “other doctrines already exist to address
concerns about competing fe deral-court and state-court
proceedings.”  But none of those other doctrines would
remedy the harm created by the suits described above:
federal suits seeking review of state civil judgments.

and deemed inapplicable in this case.  Younger abstention
applies only to pending state criminal proceedings, certain
civil enforcement proceedings, and proceedings “uniquely
in furtherance of the state courts’ ability to perform their
judicial functions.”  Sprint Commc’ns, Inc. v. Jacobs , 571
U.S. 69, 78 (2013) (citation om itted).  The district court

Dkt. 27 at 4.

460 U.S. 1, 13-14 (1983) (citation omitted).  But petitioner’s
state and federal lawsuits are not parallel because they do
not “involv[e] the contemporaneous exercise of concurrent
jurisdictions.”  Colo. River, 424 U.S. at 817.  Instead, as in

Dkt. 27 at 4-5.

II. The Court Should Reject Petitioner’s Hail-Mary Request

overrule it all.  But that is  not the question this Court
granted certiorari to review, nor was the question of

Feldman doctrine can be triggered by a state-court decision that remains subject to further review in state court.”

that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine can apply if the statecourt decision is not subject to further review.  See
